source.title: TextNCA: Neural Cellular Automata for Language Modeling via Hierarchical Local Attention
source.authors: Avni Mittal; Avinash Anand; Ashutosh Kumar; Dikshant Kukreja; Kritarth Prasad; Sushane Dulloo; Erik Cambria; Timothy Liu; Zheng-Kui Wang; R. Shah

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream-task performance for models with different pretraining perplexities and architectures, explicitly asking whether language-modelling trends transfer. It does not run a parameter, token, or compute scaling sweep.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many language-model perplexity ablations, but these vary architecture and iteration schedule rather than parameter count, training tokens, or compute as scaling-law variables. Those results do not test V1–V5 or V7. The relevant results are the downstream evaluations and their comparisons with pretraining PPL.
record.test_reason: Controlled architecture ablations test V4 at fixed or nearly fixed parameter count. Joint pretraining-PPL and downstream evaluations bear on V6, although they establish neither a fitted predictive relationship nor extrapolation across scale.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the downstream conclusion: classification is statistically tied with transformers, and QA differences track attention locality. Its summary omits the paper's main conclusion: window scheduling dominates this NCA architecture's behavior; iteration adds a bounded benefit requiring suitable gating and step conditioning, and transformers remain better at this scale, especially under matched compute. The authors claim no general downstream scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: This is an architectural study of hierarchical local-attention neural cellular automata, not a scaling-law reproduction; it evaluates downstream tasks to see whether its language-modelling trends transfer.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream outcomes differ by task and attention locality. Table 4 and Appendix B give different classification means for the same named comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: Stochastic-iteration training permits several inference iteration counts at PPL 101–108, while deterministic models degrade outside their trained horizon.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-depth robustness depends on iteration training and step conditioning; this is not a pretraining power-law or large-run extrapolation result.

record.code_released: not stated (the paper says code and configurations are released, but provides no URL)
record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The study does not perform a scale sweep or fit a relationship between pretraining loss and downstream performance. The tested models are small and differ architecturally; classification results are reported as means over three seeds, while SQuAD is single-seed. Table 4 and Appendix B give different classification values for some of the same model comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant downstream table results were intentionally left out. Rows r1–r48 cover Table 4 downstream results; r49–r50 record the additional Hier-Hybrid outcomes in Appendix B.

untested.parts: No power-law fit or controlled sweep over parameters, training tokens, or training compute across orders of magnitude.
No small-run law used to predict substantially larger training runs; iteration-horizon extrapolation is a different question.
No loss-minimising parameter/token allocation across compute budgets.
No broad depth/width aspect-ratio sweep in standard transformers, and no evidence at substantially larger model scales.
No power-law analysis in another modality or training regime. Downstream fine-tuning alone does not test the claimed functional form.
No calibrated downstream prediction, held-out prediction test, or systematic scaling relationship across orders of magnitude.

No fitted scaling exponents, compute-optimal splits, or analysis of sensitivity to scaling-law fitting choices. Architectural and iteration U-shapes alone do not establish bending of a fitted scaling law.

missing.what: Fixed-parameter schedule ablations: forward, reversed, uniform, and non-monotone schedules at 30.8M yield PPL 60.3, 131.1, 119.7, and 77.0. Record held-out cross-entropy differences as well as PPL.

Nearly fixed-parameter iteration sweep: Ts=2/4/6/8, parameters 30.83/30.84/30.86/30.87M, PPL 80.3/60.3/73.9/117.9. The table claims matched compute, but the protocol and Appendix H report equal training steps with different iteration costs; retain this inconsistency.
Learned versus sinusoidal step-conditioning LM results at approximately 30.8M: PPL 60.3 versus 119.5. Record NoStep separately with its interrupted 48k training condition.
Fixed-35.5M non-iterating window-schedule comparison: SWin-TF-Staged PPL 64.5 versus uniform-window SWin-TF PPL 63.2.
SigmoidDropout downstream comparison omitted despite the record claiming complete downstream coverage: PPL 71.7, classification average 89.8, QA F1 23.4, parameters 27.7M.

record.verdict_notes: All judgments use the supplied text. V4 was incorrectly excluded merely because architectural changes produced large effects; those effects directly bear on architecture insensitivity. PPL is exponential in cross-entropy, so architecture comparisons should report loss differences rather than treating PPL ratios as loss ratios. V6 row states use explicitly named comparisons and indicate directional agreement or failure, not validated numerical predictability. Classification averages duplicate their component tasks; SQuAD is single-seed. The supplied text does not establish the record's claimed EMNLP peer-review status.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No extrapolation from small runs to larger runs.

Architecture ablations are reported, but the study does not test whether architecture details change loss only slightly at fixed parameter count; several ablations change multiple design properties and show large PPL changes.
No other modalities, repeated-data regime, or fine-tuning/transfer power-law test.
No systematic scaling sweep or fitted relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss or scale; tested comparisons are a small set of architectures and four downstream benchmarks.
No analysis of scaling-law exponents, fit choices, or bending scaling curves.
